title: Rational–irrational constructions and Thomae’s function
section: Continuous Functions ▷ A nontrivial continuity example
terms: Thomae function; rational–irrational function; dense set; continuity via bounded denomi- nators; Dirichlet function.

exposition.text:
Thomae’s function on (0, 1) is T(x) = 0 at irrational x, and T (p/q) = 1/q for a reduced rational
p/q with q > 0. It is continuous at every irrational point and discontinuous at every rational
point. For a prescribed ε, only finitely many rationals in a bounded interval have denominator
below 1/ε; avoid those finitely many points to prove continuity at an irrational point.
Rational and irrational numbers are both dense, so a function defined by different formulas on
those two sets can be continuous only where the two limiting behaviors agree. The Dirichlet
function, equal to one on rationals and zero on irrationals, is nowhere continuous. Density and
the sequential criterion replace ordinary graph intuition for these examples.

question.text:
For Thomae’s function T on (0, 1), what is lim T(x)?
x→2/5
(A) 0
(B) 1/5
(C) 2/5
(D) 1
(E) The limit does not exist.

solution.text:
Given ε > 0, exclude all reduced rationals with denominator at most 1/ε from a punctured
neighborhood of 2/5; there are finitely many. Every remaining value of T is less than ε.
Thus the limit is zero even though T (2/5) = 1/5.

question.text:
Let f(x) = x for rational x and f(x) = 1 − x for irrational x. Where is f continuous?
(A) Only at zero
(B) Only at x = 1/2
(C) Everywhere
(D) At every rational point
(E) Nowhere

solution.text:
Both dense branches must approach the same value, requiring x = 1 − x. At 1/2 both
branches tend to 1/2, proving continuity there and nowhere else.
